book.title: Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
book.author: Robert Louis Stevenson

chapters.title: Dr. Jekyll Was Quite at Ease
Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case

questions.stem: In Enfield's story, what does Hyde do to the little girl he runs into?
choices: Tramples over her and walks on
Steals the money she carried
Pushes her into the river
Chases her across the square

evidence.quote: the man trampled calmly over the child’s body and left her screaming on the ground

questions.explanation: What shocks Enfield is how calm it is: Hyde hurts the child without any feeling at all.

questions.stem: Why is the cheque Hyde uses to pay the girl's family so suspicious?
choices: It carries the name of a respected man
It is for far too little money
It is written in a foreign language
It is dated many years earlier

evidence.quote: drawn payable to bearer and signed with a name that I can’t mention

questions.explanation: Enfield won't say the name, but it belongs to someone well known and respectable. Why would that man pay for Hyde?

questions.stem: How do people react when they see Hyde?
choices: They loathe him but can't say why
They pity him for some illness
They find him handsome and kind
They barely notice him at all

evidence.quote: he gives a strong feeling of deformity, although I couldn’t specify the point

questions.explanation: Nobody can name what's wrong with Hyde, but everyone feels it. The evil shows without being visible.

questions.stem: Why does Jekyll's will trouble Utterson so much?
choices: It gives everything to Hyde
It gives everything to Lanyon
It was never signed
It names Utterson as heir

evidence.quote: all his possessions were to pass into the hands of his “friend and benefactor Edward Hyde,”

questions.explanation: The will also gives Hyde everything if Jekyll simply disappears, which makes Utterson fear Hyde has some hold over Jekyll.

questions.stem: Utterson says of Hyde, "Something troglodytic, shall we say?" What does troglodytic mean?
choices: Like a primitive cave-dweller
Like a polite gentleman
Like a sick old man
Like a talented actor

evidence.quote: God bless me, the man seems hardly human! Something troglodytic, shall we say?

questions.explanation: Right before it, Utterson says Hyde 'seems hardly human.' A troglodyte is a cave-dweller, someone primitive and less than civilized.

questions.stem: Utterson thinks, "If he be Mr. Hyde, I shall be Mr. Seek." What does he mean?
choices: He will hunt Hyde until he finds him
He will hide from Hyde out of fear
He wants to play a game with Hyde
He will ask Jekyll to find Hyde

evidence.quote: “If he be Mr. Hyde,” he had thought, “I shall be Mr. Seek.”

questions.explanation: It's a pun on hide-and-seek. Utterson watches the door day and night until he finally meets Hyde.

questions.stem: How does Hyde kill Sir Danvers Carew?
choices: He clubs him with a heavy cane
He poisons his evening drink
He pushes him off a bridge
He shoots him in the street

evidence.quote: Mr. Hyde broke out of all bounds and clubbed him to the earth

questions.explanation: A maid sees Hyde beat the old man with a heavy stick, so hard the stick breaks.

questions.stem: Guest notices that Hyde's handwriting and Jekyll's are "in many points identical: only differently sloped." What does this suggest?
choices: Jekyll may have written as Hyde
Hyde forged Utterson's signature
Guest wrote the note himself
The note came from Lanyon

evidence.quote: the two hands are in many points identical: only differently sloped

questions.explanation: Utterson fears Jekyll forged a note for a murderer. The real answer is stranger: the same hand wrote both.

questions.stem: What does Dr. Lanyon tell Utterson has happened to him?
choices: He has had a shock he won't survive
He has caught a fever from a patient
He has lost all of his money
He has quarrelled with the police

evidence.quote: “I have had a shock,” he said, “and I shall never recover. It is a question of weeks.”

questions.explanation: Lanyon won't say what he saw. Its explanation comes later, in his letter.

questions.stem: When Utterson and Poole break into the cabinet, what is the dead Hyde wearing?
choices: Clothes far too large for him
A doctor's white coat
A soldier's uniform
A heavy black cloak

evidence.quote: He was dressed in clothes far too large for him, clothes of the doctor’s bigness

questions.explanation: Hyde is wearing Jekyll's clothes, a strong clue that the two are really one man.

questions.stem: Jekyll writes that "man is not truly one, but truly two." What idea is the novel built on?
choices: Every person has a good and an evil side
Science can make anyone a better person
Some people are simply born evil
Friendship can save a person from evil

evidence.quote: that man is not truly one, but truly two

questions.explanation: Jekyll's experiment tries to separate the two sides. Instead, the evil side takes over.

questions.stem: Why can't Jekyll make more of the drug that turns him back?
choices: The first batch had an unknown impurity
Poole refused to buy more chemicals
Lanyon burned all of his notes
The police seized his laboratory

evidence.quote: my first supply was impure, and that it was that unknown impurity which lent efficacy to the draught

questions.explanation: The new salt doesn't work. The original only worked because of an impurity he can never find again.

questions.stem: Put these events in the order they happen.

events.text: Enfield tells how Hyde trampled a child

evidence.quote: the man trampled calmly over the child’s body
“If he be Mr. Hyde,” he had thought, “I shall be Mr. Seek.”
Mr. Hyde broke out of all bounds and clubbed him to the earth

events.text: Lanyon says he has had a shock he won't recover from

evidence.quote: “I have had a shock,” he said, “and I shall never recover.”

questions.explanation: The mystery builds: a cruel act, Utterson's search, a murder, and a friend destroyed by what he saw.

questions.stem: Put these events in the order they are told.

events.text: Utterson reads that Jekyll's will leaves everything to Hyde

evidence.quote: all his possessions were to pass into the hands of his “friend and benefactor Edward Hyde,”
the two hands are in many points identical: only differently sloped

events.text: Hyde is found dead in clothes far too large

evidence.quote: He was dressed in clothes far too large for him

events.text: Jekyll writes that man is truly two

evidence.quote: that man is not truly one, but truly two

questions.explanation: The clues come first and the explanation last: the book tells the story as a mystery, with Jekyll's confession at the end.
